title: Hydrogenation safety
ends: The autoclave is in safe hands.

steps.q: What is hydrogen's flammable range in air?
steps.title: Wide range
steps.summary: Hydrogen is flammable in air from about 4 % to about 75 %, a far wider range than toluene (about 1 to 7 %), and its minimum ignition energy is only about 0.02 mJ. Assume any hydrogen leak can ignite: keep air out of the system and hydrogen in.

steps.q: Before letting hydrogen into a reactor, what must you do?
steps.title: Purge first
steps.summary: Hydrogen and air must never mix inside the reactor. Before hydrogen goes in, purge the air out with nitrogen, usually by repeated pressure-and-vent cycles, and confirm low oxygen with an analyser. At the end, purge the hydrogen out with nitrogen before opening the reactor.

draw: end: purge H₂ out with N₂

steps.q: Filtering spent palladium-on-carbon catalyst. What is the key hazard?
steps.title: Hot catalyst
steps.summary: Spent hydrogenation catalysts such as palladium on carbon hold hydrogen and are very active; if the cake dries in air it can glow and ignite the solvent. Never let it run dry, filter under nitrogen, wash with water before exposure, and store it water-wet in a closed container for metal recovery.

opts.t: It can catch fire if it dries
There is no hazard once the reaction is over

steps.q: Raising the stirrer speed makes hydrogen uptake much faster. What does that tell you?
steps.title: Mass transfer
steps.summary: Hydrogen must dissolve into the liquid before it reaches the catalyst, and its low solubility often makes this the slowest step. If faster stirring increases uptake, gas-liquid mass transfer is limiting; better dispersion, higher pressure or a gas-inducing impeller help. Faster uptake also means faster heat release.

draw: stir faster helps → mass transfer limit

steps.q: Reducing a nitro group with hydrogen is strongly exothermic. How is the heat usually controlled?
steps.title: Hydrogen is the dose
steps.summary: Reducing a nitro group to an amine releases around 130 kcal per mole. In hydrogenation, hydrogen is the dosed reagent, so the heat release is controlled through the hydrogen feed rate, using a pressure controller or flow limit interlocked to high temperature. Some nitro intermediates are thermally unstable, so check thermal data and never run hot to finish faster.

opts.t: By adding all the catalyst at once

steps.q: Where should hydrogen gas detectors be placed in a hydrogenation room?
steps.title: Detect up high
steps.summary: Hydrogen is about fourteen times lighter than air and collects under the roof, so detectors go at high points and above likely leak sources such as flanges and valves. Provide high-level ventilation and exclude ignition sources. Hydrogen flames are nearly invisible in daylight, so do not approach a suspected leak; isolate it remotely and check with a thermal camera or flame detector.

opts.t: At the high points, near the ceiling

intro.text: Hi, I'm Bubbles. Today: hydrogenation. The lightest gas, a catalyst that can catch fire on its own, and very little room for mistakes. Six questions. Ready?

outro-web.text: That's the lesson. Read the hydrogenation safety guide next.

q1.text: Question 1. What is hydrogen's flammable range in air?

q1-r0.text: That's more like toluene vapour. Hydrogen's range is huge.

q1-r1.text: 4 to 75 percent. Almost any leak can burn.

q1-r2.text: Far too narrow. Hydrogen burns across a huge range.

q1-r3.text: Far too narrow. It starts burning at just 4 percent.

q1-b0.text: Hydrogen burns in air anywhere from about 4 percent to about 75 percent.

q1-b1.text: Compare toluene vapour, about 1 to 7 percent. Hydrogen's window is enormous.

q1-b2.text: It also ignites with a tiny spark, about 0.02 millijoules. Far less than static from a person.

q1-b3.text: So assume any hydrogen leak can ignite. Keep air out of the system and hydrogen in.

q2.text: Question 2. Before letting hydrogen into a reactor, what must you do?

q2-r0.text: Slowly mixing hydrogen into air is still mixing hydrogen into air.

q2-r2.text: Heating a vessel of air and solvent vapour? Please, no.

q2-r3.text: Venting leaves the air inside. You have to push it out.

q2-b0.text: Hydrogen and air must never meet inside the reactor.

q2-b1.text: Pressurise with nitrogen, vent, and repeat. Each cycle drops the oxygen.

q2-b2.text: Check the oxygen is low enough with an analyser, typically below 1 percent, before any hydrogen goes in.

q2-b3.text: At the end, do the same in reverse: purge the hydrogen out with nitrogen before opening.

q3.text: Question 3. Filtering spent palladium-on-carbon catalyst. What is the key hazard?

q3-r0.text: Fine carbon can blind cloth, but the real danger is fire.

q3-r2.text: It stays solid. That's why you filter it.

q3-r3.text: The catalyst still holds hydrogen and is very active.

q3-b0.text: Spent hydrogenation catalysts hold hydrogen and are very active. Dry and in air, they can glow and ignite solvent.

q3-b1.text: So never let the cake run dry. Keep it covered with liquid, ideally water.

q3-b2.text: Filter under nitrogen, and wash the cake with water before it's exposed.

q3-b3.text: Store spent catalyst under water, in a closed container, and send it for metal recovery.

q4.text: Question 4. Raising the stirrer speed makes hydrogen uptake much faster. What does that tell you?

q4-r0.text: A dead catalyst wouldn't speed up with stirring.

q4-r1.text: Correct! Hydrogen can't dissolve fast enough.

q4-r2.text: A finished reaction takes up no hydrogen at all.

q4-r3.text: The uptake really changed. It's the mixing.

q4-b0.text: Hydrogen has to dissolve from the gas into the liquid before it can reach the catalyst.

q4-b1.text: Hydrogen is not very soluble, so that step is often the slowest.

q4-b2.text: If faster stirring speeds things up, mass transfer is the limit. Better gas dispersion, higher pressure, or a gas-inducing impeller help.

q4-b3.text: Watch the heat when you do: faster uptake means faster heat release.

q5.text: Question 5. Reducing a nitro group with hydrogen is strongly exothermic. How is the heat usually controlled?

q5-r0.text: Yes! Hydrogen is the dosed reagent. Limit it, and you limit heat.

q5-r1.text: That speeds it up. More heat, faster.

q5-r2.text: Cooling off during a strong exotherm? No.

q5-r3.text: Faster stirring speeds up hydrogen uptake. More heat, not less.

q5-b0.text: Nitro to amine releases a lot of heat, around 130 kilocalories per mole.

q5-b1.text: The hydrogen is the reagent you're dosing. Feed it at a rate the cooling can handle.

q5-b2.text: Use a pressure controller or a flow limit on the hydrogen, with an interlock that cuts the hydrogen on high temperature.

q5-b3.text: Nitro compounds and some reduction intermediates can be unstable. Check thermal data, and never let the batch run hot hoping it'll finish faster.

q6.text: Question 6. Where should hydrogen gas detectors be placed in a hydrogenation room?

q6-r0.text: That's for heavy vapours. Hydrogen goes the other way.

q6-r1.text: Correct! Hydrogen is very light and rises.

q6-r2.text: By then it's too late inside.

q6-r3.text: Ventilation helps. Detection tells you it's working.

q6-b0.text: Hydrogen is about fourteen times lighter than air. It rises and gathers under the roof.

q6-b1.text: So put detectors at the high points, and above likely leak spots like flanges and valves.

q6-b2.text: Give the roof a high vent so it can't build up, and keep ignition sources out.

q6-b3.text: Hydrogen flames are almost invisible in daylight. Don't walk up to a suspected leak. Isolate the supply from a distance and check with a thermal camera or flame detector. More in the hydrogenation safety guide on pharmacheme dot in.
